metadata.title: My RPG Source Rules Codex
metadata.note: Entries are concise, original summaries for play reference and are filtered by active edition where rules differ.

entries.title: Ability Score Generation
entries.summary: Ability scores can be entered manually or generated using an agreed method. The chosen numbers become the character's base Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.
entries.whatItMeans: Ability scores can be entered manually or generated using an agreed method. The chosen numbers become the character's base Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.
entries.exampleInPlay: Using 4d6 drop lowest, roll four six-sided dice, discard the lowest die, and total the other three for one score.
entries.whyItMatters: The generation method shapes a character's strengths and weaknesses before ancestry or background adjustments are applied.

entries.title: Ability Scores
entries.summary: The six ability scores describe a character's broad physical and mental capabilities.
entries.whatItMeans: The six ability scores describe a character's broad physical and mental capabilities.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Strength score of 16 produces a +3 Strength modifier.
entries.whyItMatters: Most character-sheet numbers eventually trace back to one of the six ability scores.

entries.title: Ability Modifier
entries.summary: An ability modifier is derived from an ability score and is the number usually added to related rolls.
entries.whatItMeans: An ability modifier is derived from an ability score and is the number usually added to related rolls.
entries.exampleInPlay: A score of 14 or 15 gives a +2 modifier; a score of 8 or 9 gives a -1 modifier.
entries.whyItMatters: The modifier, rather than the full score, is used in most moment-to-moment play.

entries.title: Class and Level
entries.summary: A class describes the main adventuring path a character follows, while level measures progress in that class.
entries.whatItMeans: A class describes the main adventuring path a character follows, while level measures progress in that class.
entries.exampleInPlay: A level 3 Fighter has the features granted by the Fighter class through level 3.
entries.whyItMatters: Class and level determine most of a character's advancing abilities.

entries.title: Multiclassing
entries.summary: Multiclassing divides character levels between two or more classes, subject to the edition's prerequisites and rules.
entries.whatItMeans: Multiclassing divides character levels between two or more classes, subject to the edition's prerequisites and rules.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Fighter 3 / Wizard 2 is a level 5 character with levels in two classes.
entries.whyItMatters: Multiclassing creates flexible combinations but can delay stronger features from a single class.

entries.title: Race (2014)
entries.summary: In the 2014 rules, Race supplies inherited traits and commonly changes ability scores, speed, and special abilities.
entries.whatItMeans: In the 2014 rules, Race supplies inherited traits and commonly changes ability scores, speed, and special abilities.
entries.exampleInPlay: Choosing Hill Dwarf applies its listed bonuses and traits to the character.
entries.whyItMatters: Race is one of the major mechanical foundations of a 2014 character.

entries.title: Race Traits (2014)
entries.summary: Race traits are the special senses, resistances, proficiencies, movement options, and other features granted by a 2014 Race.
entries.whatItMeans: Race traits are the special senses, resistances, proficiencies, movement options, and other features granted by a 2014 Race.
entries.exampleInPlay: Darkvision lets a character see in darkness within the trait's listed range.
entries.whyItMatters: These traits can matter as much as the Race's ability-score bonuses.

entries.title: Species (2024)
entries.summary: In the 2024 rules, Species grants physical and supernatural traits such as speed, senses, resistances, and lineage choices. Ability-score increases come from Background instead.
entries.whatItMeans: In the 2024 rules, Species grants physical and supernatural traits such as speed, senses, resistances, and lineage choices. Ability-score increases come from Background instead.
entries.exampleInPlay: Choosing Elf grants Elf traits and asks for an Elven Lineage choice.
entries.whyItMatters: Keeping Species traits separate from Background ability scores is a central 2024 character-creation rule.

entries.title: Species Choices (2024)
entries.summary: Some 2024 Species require a choice such as lineage, ancestry, size, skill, feat, or spellcasting ability.
entries.whatItMeans: Some 2024 Species require a choice such as lineage, ancestry, size, skill, feat, or spellcasting ability.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Wood Elf lineage changes the character's Speed and grants its listed lineage magic.
entries.whyItMatters: These selections finish the Species package and should be recorded with the character.

entries.title: Background (2014)
entries.summary: A 2014 Background describes the life a character led before adventuring and grants proficiencies, equipment, languages, and a feature.
entries.whatItMeans: A 2014 Background describes the life a character led before adventuring and grants proficiencies, equipment, languages, and a feature.
entries.exampleInPlay: An Acolyte begins with the Background's listed proficiencies, equipment, and feature.
entries.whyItMatters: Background adds practical training and story hooks without supplying ability-score increases.

entries.title: Background (2024)
entries.summary: A 2024 Background grants ability-score options, an Origin feat, skill proficiencies, a tool proficiency, and starting equipment.
entries.whatItMeans: A 2024 Background grants ability-score options, an Origin feat, skill proficiencies, a tool proficiency, and starting equipment.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Soldier chooses its permitted ability increases and gains the Background's listed feat and proficiencies.
entries.whyItMatters: Background now carries much of the mechanical weight that Race carried in the 2014 rules.

entries.title: Background Ability Scores (2024)
entries.summary: A 2024 Background offers three eligible abilities. Increase one by 2 and another by 1, or increase all three by 1, without raising a score above the normal character-creation limit.
entries.whatItMeans: A 2024 Background offers three eligible abilities. Increase one by 2 and another by 1, or increase all three by 1, without raising a score above the normal character-creation limit.
entries.exampleInPlay: Acolyte can place +2 in Wisdom and +1 in Charisma, or +1 in each of its three listed abilities.
entries.whyItMatters: These increases replace the old 2014 Race-based ability bonuses.

entries.title: Alignment
entries.summary: Alignment is a broad roleplaying description of a character's moral outlook and relationship with order, freedom, good, and evil.
entries.whatItMeans: Alignment is a broad roleplaying description of a character's moral outlook and relationship with order, freedom, good, and evil.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Lawful Good character might value duty and compassion, but still disagree with another Lawful Good character about the right action.
entries.whyItMatters: Alignment is a guide, not a script. Personality and choices remain more specific.
bestFor: Players using alignment as a roleplaying aid

entries.title: Experience Points
entries.summary: Experience Points, or XP, are one method for tracking progress toward the next character level.
entries.whatItMeans: Experience Points, or XP, are one method for tracking progress toward the next character level.
entries.exampleInPlay: When the campaign awards enough XP to reach the next threshold, the character gains a level.
entries.whyItMatters: Some campaigns use XP while others use milestone advancement.

entries.title: Personality, Ideals, Bonds, and Flaws
entries.summary: These notes describe how a character behaves, what they believe, what they care about, and where they are vulnerable.
entries.whatItMeans: These notes describe how a character behaves, what they believe, what they care about, and where they are vulnerable.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character might be generous to strangers, devoted to a lost sibling, and dangerously unwilling to retreat.
entries.whyItMatters: Specific character details make roleplaying easier than relying on alignment alone.

entries.title: Class Abilities and Feats
entries.summary: This section records the class features, feats, fighting styles, invocations, maneuvers, and other special abilities the character can use.
entries.whatItMeans: This section records the class features, feats, fighting styles, invocations, maneuvers, and other special abilities the character can use.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Fighter might record Action Surge and Second Wind, including how often each can be used.
entries.whyItMatters: Writing the feature name and its key limit makes the paper sheet much faster to use.

entries.title: Strength
entries.summary: Strength measures physical power, force, and raw muscle.
entries.whatItMeans: Strength measures physical power, force, and raw muscle.
entries.exampleInPlay: A high-Strength character might force open a barred door or wrestle an enemy.
entries.whyItMatters: Strength is important whenever a roll or rule calls for its modifier.

entries.title: Dexterity
entries.summary: Dexterity measures agility, reflexes, balance, and fine control.
entries.whatItMeans: Dexterity measures agility, reflexes, balance, and fine control.
entries.exampleInPlay: A high-Dexterity character might dodge a trap, sneak quietly, or fire a bow accurately.
entries.whyItMatters: Dexterity is important whenever a roll or rule calls for its modifier.

entries.title: Constitution
entries.summary: Constitution measures toughness, health, and endurance.
entries.whatItMeans: Constitution measures toughness, health, and endurance.
entries.exampleInPlay: A high-Constitution character can endure more damage and maintain spells more reliably.
entries.whyItMatters: Constitution is important whenever a roll or rule calls for its modifier.

entries.exampleInPlay: A high-Intelligence character might identify a rune or reconstruct events from evidence.
entries.whyItMatters: Intelligence is important whenever a roll or rule calls for its modifier.

entries.whyItMatters: Wisdom is important whenever a roll or rule calls for its modifier.

entries.whyItMatters: Charisma is important whenever a roll or rule calls for its modifier.

entries.whatItMeans: Acrobatics is a Dexterity-based skill covering balance, tumbling, and controlled movement.
entries.exampleInPlay: Keep your footing on a slick rooftop.
entries.whyItMatters: Proficiency adds the character's Proficiency Bonus when the check uses Acrobatics.

entries.whatItMeans: Sleight of Hand is a Dexterity-based skill covering subtle hand movements and quick-fingered manipulation.
entries.exampleInPlay: Slip a key from a belt without being noticed.
entries.whyItMatters: Proficiency adds the character's Proficiency Bonus when the check uses Sleight of Hand.

entries.whatItMeans: Stealth is a Dexterity-based skill covering hiding, moving quietly, and avoiding notice.
entries.exampleInPlay: Move through a guarded hallway unseen.
entries.whyItMatters: Proficiency adds the character's Proficiency Bonus when the check uses Stealth.

entries.whatItMeans: Survival is a Wisdom-based skill covering tracking, navigation, foraging, and wilderness travel.
entries.exampleInPlay: Follow tracks through a forest after rainfall.
entries.whyItMatters: Proficiency adds the character's Proficiency Bonus when the check uses Survival.

entries.title: Skill Checks
entries.summary: A skill check is an ability check associated with a trained area such as Stealth, Perception, or Arcana.
entries.whatItMeans: A skill check is an ability check associated with a trained area such as Stealth, Perception, or Arcana.
entries.exampleInPlay: A proficient character adds both the relevant ability modifier and Proficiency Bonus.
entries.whyItMatters: Skills describe common applications of the six abilities.

entries.title: Saving Throws
entries.summary: A saving throw is a defensive roll made to resist or avoid a harmful effect.
entries.whatItMeans: A saving throw is a defensive roll made to resist or avoid a harmful effect.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Dexterity save might reduce the damage from an explosion.
entries.whyItMatters: Saving-throw proficiency adds Proficiency Bonus to saves using that ability.

entries.title: Strength Saving Throw
entries.summary: This save is commonly used for being pushed, pulled, restrained, or physically overpowered.
entries.whatItMeans: This save is commonly used for being pushed, pulled, restrained, or physically overpowered.
whatItAffects: Defensive rolls using the listed ability
Proficiency if the character is trained in the save
entries.exampleInPlay: Roll a d20, add the relevant ability modifier, and add Proficiency Bonus if proficient.
entries.whyItMatters: Different threats call for different saving throws.

entries.title: Dexterity Saving Throw
entries.summary: This save is commonly used for dodging sudden hazards, blasts, traps, and area effects.
entries.whatItMeans: This save is commonly used for dodging sudden hazards, blasts, traps, and area effects.
whatItAffects: Defensive rolls using the listed ability
Proficiency if the character is trained in the save
entries.exampleInPlay: Roll a d20, add the relevant ability modifier, and add Proficiency Bonus if proficient.
entries.whyItMatters: Different threats call for different saving throws.

entries.title: Constitution Saving Throw
entries.summary: This save is commonly used for enduring poison, disease, extreme strain, and maintaining Concentration.
entries.whatItMeans: This save is commonly used for enduring poison, disease, extreme strain, and maintaining Concentration.
whatItAffects: Defensive rolls using the listed ability
Proficiency if the character is trained in the save
entries.exampleInPlay: Roll a d20, add the relevant ability modifier, and add Proficiency Bonus if proficient.
entries.whyItMatters: Different threats call for different saving throws.

entries.whatItMeans: This save is commonly used for resisting effects that assault reasoning, memory, or the mind's structure.
whatItAffects: Defensive rolls using the listed ability
Proficiency if the character is trained in the save
entries.exampleInPlay: Roll a d20, add the relevant ability modifier, and add Proficiency Bonus if proficient.
entries.whyItMatters: Different threats call for different saving throws.

whatItAffects: Defensive rolls using the listed ability
Proficiency if the character is trained in the save
entries.exampleInPlay: Roll a d20, add the relevant ability modifier, and add Proficiency Bonus if proficient.

entries.summary: This save is commonly used for resisting effects that displace, possess, banish, or overpower a creature's presence.
entries.whatItMeans: This save is commonly used for resisting effects that displace, possess, banish, or overpower a creature's presence.
whatItAffects: Defensive rolls using the listed ability
Proficiency if the character is trained in the save
entries.exampleInPlay: Roll a d20, add the relevant ability modifier, and add Proficiency Bonus if proficient.
entries.whyItMatters: Different threats call for different saving throws.

entries.title: Armor Class
entries.summary: Armor Class, or AC, is the target number an attack roll must meet or exceed to hit.
entries.whatItMeans: Armor Class, or AC, is the target number an attack roll must meet or exceed to hit.
entries.exampleInPlay: An attack total of 17 hits AC 16.
entries.whyItMatters: Higher AC makes weapon and spell attacks less likely to hit.

entries.title: Initiative
entries.summary: Initiative determines turn order when combat begins.
entries.whatItMeans: Initiative determines turn order when combat begins.
entries.exampleInPlay: Each participant rolls initiative, usually using Dexterity.
entries.whyItMatters: Acting earlier can change positioning and protect allies.

entries.title: Speed
entries.summary: Speed is the distance a character can move on a turn, normally measured in feet.
entries.whatItMeans: Speed is the distance a character can move on a turn, normally measured in feet.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Speed of 30 feet allows up to 30 feet of normal movement on the turn.
entries.whyItMatters: Position often decides which targets and objectives a character can reach.

entries.title: Hit Points
entries.summary: Hit Points, or HP, measure how much damage a character can sustain before dropping to 0 HP.
entries.whatItMeans: Hit Points, or HP, measure how much damage a character can sustain before dropping to 0 HP.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character at 12 HP who takes 7 damage has 5 HP left.
entries.whyItMatters: HP is the clearest measure of immediate endurance in combat.

entries.title: Temporary Hit Points
entries.summary: Temporary Hit Points are a buffer that is lost before normal HP. Multiple sources do not normally stack; keep the higher amount.
entries.whatItMeans: Temporary Hit Points are a buffer that is lost before normal HP. Multiple sources do not normally stack; keep the higher amount.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character with 5 temporary HP who takes 8 damage loses the temporary HP and takes 3 normal damage.
entries.whyItMatters: They protect a character without counting as healing.

entries.title: Hit Dice
entries.summary: Hit Dice are class-based dice used for calculating HP and commonly for recovering HP during a Short Rest.
entries.whatItMeans: Hit Dice are class-based dice used for calculating HP and commonly for recovering HP during a Short Rest.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Fighter normally uses a d10 Hit Die for Fighter levels.
entries.whyItMatters: Multiclass characters may track more than one Hit Die type.

entries.title: Death Saving Throws
entries.summary: At 0 HP, a character normally makes a Death Saving Throw at the start of each turn. Three successes stabilize; three failures cause death.
entries.whatItMeans: At 0 HP, a character normally makes a Death Saving Throw at the start of each turn. Three successes stabilize; three failures cause death.
entries.exampleInPlay: A roll of 10 or higher is normally a success. A natural 1 counts as two failures, while a natural 20 restores 1 HP.
entries.whyItMatters: Death saves create a short, dangerous window for allies to help.

entries.title: Proficiency Bonus
entries.summary: Proficiency Bonus is added when the character is trained in a save, skill, weapon, tool, or other rule that grants proficiency.
entries.whatItMeans: Proficiency Bonus is added when the character is trained in a save, skill, weapon, tool, or other rule that grants proficiency.
entries.exampleInPlay: A proficient skill with a +3 ability modifier and +2 Proficiency Bonus has a +5 total.
entries.whyItMatters: It scales with total character level and powers many core calculations.

entries.title: Passive Perception
entries.summary: Passive Perception represents what a character notices without making an active roll.
entries.whatItMeans: Passive Perception represents what a character notices without making an active roll.
entries.exampleInPlay: A hidden danger can be compared against the character's Passive Perception.
entries.whyItMatters: It lets the GM resolve awareness without repeatedly asking for rolls.

entries.title: Attack Rolls
entries.summary: An attack roll is a d20 roll plus the relevant ability modifier and Proficiency Bonus when proficient.
entries.whatItMeans: An attack roll is a d20 roll plus the relevant ability modifier and Proficiency Bonus when proficient.
entries.exampleInPlay: A +5 attack bonus and a roll of 12 produce a total of 17.
entries.whyItMatters: Attack rolls are the most common way to resolve attempts to hit a target.

entries.title: Attack Bonus
entries.summary: Attack Bonus is the total modifier added to an attack roll.
entries.whatItMeans: Attack Bonus is the total modifier added to an attack roll.
entries.exampleInPlay: A proficient Strength weapon attack might add Strength modifier plus Proficiency Bonus.
entries.whyItMatters: Recording the final bonus speeds up every attack.

entries.title: Melee Attacks
entries.summary: Melee attacks target creatures within the weapon or effect's reach.
entries.whatItMeans: Melee attacks target creatures within the weapon or effect's reach.
entries.exampleInPlay: A longsword normally attacks a target within 5 feet.
entries.whyItMatters: Melee positioning can expose a character to retaliation and opportunity attacks.

entries.title: Ranged Attacks
entries.summary: Ranged attacks target at a distance and normally use the weapon or spell's listed range.
entries.whatItMeans: Ranged attacks target at a distance and normally use the weapon or spell's listed range.
entries.exampleInPlay: A bow can attack a distant target, with penalties or restrictions beyond normal range.
entries.whyItMatters: Range allows safer positioning but can be affected by cover and nearby enemies.

entries.title: Damage Rolls
entries.summary: A damage roll determines how much HP an attack or effect removes after it hits or takes effect.
entries.whatItMeans: A damage roll determines how much HP an attack or effect removes after it hits or takes effect.
entries.exampleInPlay: A weapon might deal 1d8 plus an ability modifier.
entries.whyItMatters: Damage type and dice can interact with resistances, vulnerabilities, and critical hits.

entries.title: Critical Hits
entries.summary: A critical hit normally rolls the attack's damage dice twice, then adds modifiers once.
entries.whatItMeans: A critical hit normally rolls the attack's damage dice twice, then adds modifiers once.
entries.exampleInPlay: A 1d8 weapon with a +3 modifier normally deals 2d8 + 3 on a critical hit.
entries.whyItMatters: Critical hits create sudden damage spikes.

entries.title: Actions
entries.summary: On a turn, a creature normally takes one Action, which can be used for options such as Attack, Dash, Disengage, Dodge, Help, Hide, Ready, Search, or Use an Object.
entries.whatItMeans: On a turn, a creature normally takes one Action, which can be used for options such as Attack, Dash, Disengage, Dodge, Help, Hide, Ready, Search, or Use an Object.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character can use the Attack action to make attacks allowed by their features.
entries.whyItMatters: The Action is the main decision of most turns.

entries.title: Bonus Actions
entries.summary: A Bonus Action is an additional option available only when a feature, spell, or rule says it can be used as one.
entries.whatItMeans: A Bonus Action is an additional option available only when a feature, spell, or rule says it can be used as one.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Rogue might use Cunning Action as a Bonus Action.
entries.whyItMatters: You cannot invent a Bonus Action; a rule must grant one.

entries.title: Reactions
entries.summary: A Reaction is a quick response to a trigger. A creature normally has one Reaction available until the start of its next turn.
entries.whatItMeans: A Reaction is a quick response to a trigger. A creature normally has one Reaction available until the start of its next turn.
entries.exampleInPlay: Leaving an enemy's reach can trigger an opportunity attack using a Reaction.
entries.whyItMatters: Using a Reaction now may leave it unavailable for another trigger.

entries.title: Opportunity Attacks
entries.summary: An opportunity attack is a Reaction triggered when a visible enemy willingly leaves your reach without using a rule that prevents it.
entries.whatItMeans: An opportunity attack is a Reaction triggered when a visible enemy willingly leaves your reach without using a rule that prevents it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A creature moving away from a sword-wielding enemy may provoke an attack before leaving reach.
entries.whyItMatters: Threatened movement can shape positioning and escape choices.

entries.title: Movement
entries.summary: A creature can move up to its Speed during its turn and can split that movement around actions when permitted.
entries.whatItMeans: A creature can move up to its Speed during its turn and can split that movement around actions when permitted.
entries.exampleInPlay: Move 10 feet, attack, then move the remaining 20 feet of a 30-foot Speed.
entries.whyItMatters: Movement is separate from the Action but can trigger hazards or opportunity attacks.

entries.title: Difficult Terrain
entries.summary: Each foot of movement through difficult terrain normally costs an extra foot of movement.
entries.whatItMeans: Each foot of movement through difficult terrain normally costs an extra foot of movement.
entries.exampleInPlay: Moving 10 feet through difficult terrain usually costs 20 feet of Speed.
entries.whyItMatters: Terrain can make a short route more expensive than a longer clear route.

entries.title: Cover
entries.summary: Cover protects a target behind an obstacle. Half cover grants +2 AC and Dexterity saves, three-quarters cover grants +5, and total cover prevents direct targeting by many effects.
entries.whatItMeans: Cover protects a target behind an obstacle. Half cover grants +2 AC and Dexterity saves, three-quarters cover grants +5, and total cover prevents direct targeting by many effects.
entries.exampleInPlay: A low wall might provide half cover against an archer.
entries.whyItMatters: Using the environment can be as valuable as wearing better armor.

entries.title: Short Rest

entries.title: Conditions

entries.title: Exhaustion (2014)
entries.summary: 2014 Exhaustion has six cumulative levels: Disadvantage on ability checks; Speed halved; Disadvantage on attacks and saves; HP maximum halved; Speed 0; death.
entries.whatItMeans: 2014 Exhaustion has six cumulative levels: Disadvantage on ability checks; Speed halved; Disadvantage on attacks and saves; HP maximum halved; Speed 0; death.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character at level 3 has the effects of levels 1, 2, and 3.
entries.whyItMatters: Exhaustion becomes rapidly dangerous because every level adds another effect.

entries.title: Exhaustion (2024)
entries.summary: 2024 Exhaustion applies a -2 penalty to D20 Tests per level and reduces Speed by 5 feet per level. Reaching level 6 causes death.
entries.whatItMeans: 2024 Exhaustion applies a -2 penalty to D20 Tests per level and reduces Speed by 5 feet per level. Reaching level 6 causes death.

entries.whyItMatters: The penalty scales predictably but becomes severe after only a few levels.

entries.title: Equipment Inventory
entries.summary: The equipment list records weapons, armor, tools, adventuring gear, consumables, and important carried objects.
entries.whatItMeans: The equipment list records weapons, armor, tools, adventuring gear, consumables, and important carried objects.
entries.exampleInPlay: Record a rope, healing potion, shield, and thieves' tools where they can be found quickly.
entries.whyItMatters: A paper character can only use equipment the player remembers having.

entries.title: Currency
entries.summary: Currency is recorded by coin type: copper pieces (CP), silver pieces (SP), electrum pieces (EP), gold pieces (GP), and platinum pieces (PP).
entries.whatItMeans: Currency is recorded by coin type: copper pieces (CP), silver pieces (SP), electrum pieces (EP), gold pieces (GP), and platinum pieces (PP).
entries.exampleInPlay: A Background grant of 8 GP belongs in the GP field rather than the inventory text.
entries.whyItMatters: Keeping denominations separate prevents equipment text and money totals from becoming tangled.

entries.title: Carrying Capacity
entries.summary: Carrying capacity is normally based on Strength and determines how much weight a character can carry before optional encumbrance rules apply.
entries.whatItMeans: Carrying capacity is normally based on Strength and determines how much weight a character can carry before optional encumbrance rules apply.
entries.exampleInPlay: A stronger character can usually carry more gear without difficulty.
entries.whyItMatters: Weight matters when treasure, armor, and supplies accumulate.

entries.title: Tool Proficiency
entries.summary: Tool proficiency represents training with a tool set, instrument, vehicle, or craft. Add Proficiency Bonus when the rules call for a relevant proficient check.
entries.whatItMeans: Tool proficiency represents training with a tool set, instrument, vehicle, or craft. Add Proficiency Bonus when the rules call for a relevant proficient check.
entries.exampleInPlay: Thieves' tools proficiency can apply when picking a lock with those tools.
entries.whyItMatters: Tools create useful options that are not covered by ordinary skills alone.

entries.title: Adventuring Gear
entries.summary: Adventuring gear includes practical items such as rope, torches, containers, kits, rations, and specialized supplies.
entries.whatItMeans: Adventuring gear includes practical items such as rope, torches, containers, kits, rations, and specialized supplies.
entries.exampleInPlay: A rope can solve a climbing problem without requiring a special class feature.
entries.whyItMatters: Creative equipment use often turns a difficult obstacle into a manageable one.

entries.title: Weapons
entries.summary: A weapon entry provides damage, damage type, properties, and whether it is a simple or martial weapon.
entries.whatItMeans: A weapon entry provides damage, damage type, properties, and whether it is a simple or martial weapon.
entries.exampleInPlay: A longsword deals its listed damage and can use its Versatile property when held in two hands.
entries.whyItMatters: Choose weapons the character is proficient with and record the final attack and damage modifiers.

entries.title: Weapon Proficiency
entries.summary: Weapon proficiency allows the character to add Proficiency Bonus to attack rolls with that weapon.
entries.whatItMeans: Weapon proficiency allows the character to add Proficiency Bonus to attack rolls with that weapon.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Fighter normally adds Proficiency Bonus to attacks with weapons covered by the class's proficiencies.
entries.whyItMatters: Lacking proficiency does not normally prevent an attack, but it lowers accuracy.

entries.title: Weapon Properties
entries.summary: Weapon properties describe special handling rules such as Finesse, Light, Heavy, Reach, Thrown, Two-Handed, Versatile, Ammunition, or Loading.
entries.whatItMeans: Weapon properties describe special handling rules such as Finesse, Light, Heavy, Reach, Thrown, Two-Handed, Versatile, Ammunition, or Loading.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Finesse weapon can use Strength or Dexterity for the attack and damage rolls.
entries.whyItMatters: Properties often matter more than the weapon's damage die when choosing a fighting style.

entries.title: Finesse
entries.summary: A Finesse weapon can use Strength or Dexterity for its attack and damage rolls; use the same ability for both.
entries.whatItMeans: A Finesse weapon can use Strength or Dexterity for its attack and damage rolls; use the same ability for both.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Rogue can use Dexterity with a rapier.
entries.whyItMatters: Finesse supports agile melee characters.

entries.title: Light Weapons
entries.summary: Light weapons are easy to handle together and interact with the edition's rules for fighting with two weapons.
entries.whatItMeans: Light weapons are easy to handle together and interact with the edition's rules for fighting with two weapons.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character wielding two light weapons may qualify for an additional attack under the relevant rules.
entries.whyItMatters: Check the active edition and features for the exact action cost and modifier rules.

entries.title: Heavy Weapons
entries.summary: Heavy weapons are bulky, and Small or Tiny creatures may face restrictions or Disadvantage when using them, depending on the active edition.
entries.whatItMeans: Heavy weapons are bulky, and Small or Tiny creatures may face restrictions or Disadvantage when using them, depending on the active edition.
entries.exampleInPlay: A greatsword carries the Heavy and Two-Handed properties.
entries.whyItMatters: The property can limit which characters use the weapon effectively.

entries.title: Two-Handed
entries.summary: A Two-Handed weapon requires two hands when making an attack with it.
entries.whatItMeans: A Two-Handed weapon requires two hands when making an attack with it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A greatsword cannot be used to attack while the other hand holds a shield.
entries.whyItMatters: Hand requirements affect equipment combinations.

entries.title: Versatile
entries.summary: A Versatile weapon has a second damage die used when the weapon is wielded with two hands.
entries.whatItMeans: A Versatile weapon has a second damage die used when the weapon is wielded with two hands.
entries.exampleInPlay: A longsword uses its one-handed die normally and its larger Versatile die in two hands.
entries.whyItMatters: Versatile weapons trade shield use for more damage.

entries.title: Ammunition
entries.summary: A weapon with the Ammunition property consumes the listed ammunition and normally requires a free hand to load it.
entries.whatItMeans: A weapon with the Ammunition property consumes the listed ammunition and normally requires a free hand to load it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A longbow shot uses an arrow.
entries.whyItMatters: Tracking ammunition matters in survival-focused or resource-heavy games.

entries.title: Loading
entries.summary: The Loading property limits how many pieces of ammunition can be fired from that weapon when using an Action, Bonus Action, or Reaction, regardless of extra attacks, unless another rule overrides it.
entries.whatItMeans: The Loading property limits how many pieces of ammunition can be fired from that weapon when using an Action, Bonus Action, or Reaction, regardless of extra attacks, unless another rule overrides it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A crossbow with Loading may not benefit from every extra attack without a feature that ignores Loading.
entries.whyItMatters: Loading can strongly affect high-level martial characters.

entries.title: Thrown
entries.summary: A Thrown weapon can make a ranged attack using the same ability normally used for its melee attack, unless another rule changes it.
entries.whatItMeans: A Thrown weapon can make a ranged attack using the same ability normally used for its melee attack, unless another rule changes it.
entries.exampleInPlay: A handaxe can be thrown using Strength.
entries.whyItMatters: Thrown weapons give melee characters a short-range option.

entries.title: Weapon Mastery (2024)
entries.summary: Weapon Mastery allows qualifying 2024 characters to use a weapon's Mastery property, such as Cleave, Graze, Nick, Push, Sap, Slow, Topple, or Vex.
entries.whatItMeans: Weapon Mastery allows qualifying 2024 characters to use a weapon's Mastery property, such as Cleave, Graze, Nick, Push, Sap, Slow, Topple, or Vex.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character with mastery in a Vex weapon can gain the property's listed advantage-setting effect after a hit.
entries.whyItMatters: Mastery gives weapons distinct tactical identities beyond damage dice.

entries.title: Armor
entries.summary: Armor determines a base Armor Class formula and may limit how Dexterity contributes.
entries.whatItMeans: Armor determines a base Armor Class formula and may limit how Dexterity contributes.
entries.exampleInPlay: Medium armor normally uses a limited Dexterity contribution, while heavy armor normally ignores Dexterity.
entries.whyItMatters: Armor choice balances defense, proficiencies, cost, weight, and stealth.

entries.title: Armor Proficiency
entries.summary: Armor proficiency represents training to wear an armor category effectively. Wearing armor without proficiency imposes serious restrictions.
entries.whatItMeans: Armor proficiency represents training to wear an armor category effectively. Wearing armor without proficiency imposes serious restrictions.
entries.exampleInPlay: A class proficient with medium armor can wear it without the nonproficiency penalties.
entries.whyItMatters: High AC is not useful if the character cannot function properly in the armor.

entries.title: Light Armor
entries.summary: Light armor uses its listed base AC plus the wearer's full Dexterity modifier.
entries.whatItMeans: Light armor uses its listed base AC plus the wearer's full Dexterity modifier.
entries.exampleInPlay: Studded leather uses its base AC plus Dexterity modifier.
entries.whyItMatters: Light armor rewards high Dexterity and usually avoids Stealth Disadvantage.

entries.title: Medium Armor
entries.summary: Medium armor uses its listed base AC plus a limited amount of Dexterity modifier, normally no more than +2.
entries.whatItMeans: Medium armor uses its listed base AC plus a limited amount of Dexterity modifier, normally no more than +2.
entries.exampleInPlay: A character with +4 Dexterity normally adds only +2 while wearing standard medium armor.
entries.whyItMatters: Medium armor provides solid defense without requiring the highest Strength.

entries.title: Heavy Armor
entries.summary: Heavy armor uses its listed AC without adding Dexterity. Some suits have Strength requirements and impose Stealth Disadvantage.
entries.whatItMeans: Heavy armor uses its listed AC without adding Dexterity. Some suits have Strength requirements and impose Stealth Disadvantage.
entries.exampleInPlay: Plate provides its listed AC whether Dexterity is high or low.
entries.whyItMatters: Heavy armor offers strong predictable defense for trained characters.

entries.title: Shields
entries.summary: A shield occupies one hand and normally increases Armor Class while worn, provided the character is proficient.
entries.whatItMeans: A shield occupies one hand and normally increases Armor Class while worn, provided the character is proficient.
entries.exampleInPlay: A sword-and-shield character gains the shield's AC bonus but cannot use a Two-Handed weapon at the same time.
entries.whyItMatters: Shields trade hand flexibility for defense.

entries.title: Spellcasting
entries.summary: Spellcasting uses class or feature rules to cast spells, usually involving a spellcasting ability, components, range, duration, and sometimes spell slots.
entries.whatItMeans: Spellcasting uses class or feature rules to cast spells, usually involving a spellcasting ability, components, range, duration, and sometimes spell slots.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Wizard uses Intelligence for Wizard spells.
entries.whyItMatters: Recording the key statistics prevents repeated rulebook searches.

entries.title: Spellcasting Ability
entries.summary: A spellcasting ability is the ability used to calculate a character's spell attack bonus and Spell Save DC for a particular source of magic.
entries.whatItMeans: A spellcasting ability is the ability used to calculate a character's spell attack bonus and Spell Save DC for a particular source of magic.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Cleric normally uses Wisdom for Cleric spells.
entries.whyItMatters: Multiclass characters can have more than one spellcasting ability.

entries.title: Spell Save DC
entries.summary: Spell Save DC is the target number a creature must meet or exceed on a saving throw against the character's spell.
entries.whatItMeans: Spell Save DC is the target number a creature must meet or exceed on a saving throw against the character's spell.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Spell Save DC of 14 requires a saving throw total of 14 or higher to succeed.
entries.whyItMatters: A higher DC makes save-based spells harder to resist.

entries.title: Spell Attack Bonus
entries.summary: Spell Attack Bonus is added to spell attack rolls and normally equals Proficiency Bonus plus the relevant spellcasting ability modifier.
entries.whatItMeans: Spell Attack Bonus is added to spell attack rolls and normally equals Proficiency Bonus plus the relevant spellcasting ability modifier.
entries.exampleInPlay: A +3 spellcasting modifier and +2 Proficiency Bonus produce a +5 spell attack bonus.
entries.whyItMatters: Attack spells use this number instead of a weapon attack bonus.

entries.title: Cantrips
entries.summary: Cantrips are level 0 spells that can normally be cast without expending spell slots.
entries.whatItMeans: Cantrips are level 0 spells that can normally be cast without expending spell slots.
entries.exampleInPlay: A spellcaster can cast a known or prepared cantrip repeatedly unless another rule limits it.
entries.whyItMatters: Cantrips provide reliable magic when spell slots are scarce.

entries.title: Spell Slots
entries.summary: Spell slots are resources spent to cast leveled spells. A slot's level must be at least the spell's level.
entries.whatItMeans: Spell slots are resources spent to cast leveled spells. A slot's level must be at least the spell's level.
entries.exampleInPlay: A 1st-level spell can be cast using a 1st-level or higher slot.
entries.whyItMatters: Slots are a spellcaster's primary limited resource.

entries.title: Prepared and Known Spells
entries.summary: A class or feature determines which spells a character knows or prepares and how that list can change.
entries.whatItMeans: A class or feature determines which spells a character knows or prepares and how that list can change.
entries.exampleInPlay: A prepared caster selects spells from the class list according to its preparation rule.
entries.whyItMatters: Spell slots are useless without an available spell to cast with them.

entries.title: Concentration
entries.summary: A creature can normally concentrate on only one effect at a time. Taking damage can require a Constitution save with DC 10 or half the damage taken, whichever is higher.
entries.whatItMeans: A creature can normally concentrate on only one effect at a time. Taking damage can require a Constitution save with DC 10 or half the damage taken, whichever is higher.
entries.exampleInPlay: Taking 22 damage while concentrating normally calls for a DC 11 Constitution save.
entries.whyItMatters: Starting another Concentration effect ends the first, so timing matters.

entries.title: Ritual Casting
entries.summary: A spell with the Ritual tag can be cast as a ritual by a character whose feature allows it, adding time but usually avoiding a spell-slot cost.
entries.whatItMeans: A spell with the Ritual tag can be cast as a ritual by a character whose feature allows it, adding time but usually avoiding a spell-slot cost.
entries.exampleInPlay: A ritual-capable caster can cast a prepared ritual without spending a slot by taking the extra time.
entries.whyItMatters: Rituals preserve slots when time is available.

entries.title: Spell Components
entries.summary: Spell components describe what casting requires: verbal words, somatic gestures, and material objects or a spellcasting focus.
entries.whatItMeans: Spell components describe what casting requires: verbal words, somatic gestures, and material objects or a spellcasting focus.
entries.exampleInPlay: A spell with somatic components may require a free hand unless another rule allows the hand to hold a focus or material component.
entries.whyItMatters: Components determine whether a character can cast in unusual situations.

entries.title: Casting Time
entries.summary: Casting Time states whether a spell uses an Action, Bonus Action, Reaction, minute, hour, or another amount of time.
entries.whatItMeans: Casting Time states whether a spell uses an Action, Bonus Action, Reaction, minute, hour, or another amount of time.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Reaction spell can only be cast when its trigger occurs.
entries.whyItMatters: A powerful spell may be unusable when there is not enough time to cast it.

entries.title: Spell Range
entries.summary: Range states where a spell can originate or which targets it can affect. Self, Touch, and measured distances use different targeting limits.
entries.whatItMeans: Range states where a spell can originate or which targets it can affect. Self, Touch, and measured distances use different targeting limits.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Touch spell normally requires the caster to reach the target.
entries.whyItMatters: Range determines whether positioning permits the spell at all.

entries.title: Spell Duration
entries.summary: Duration states how long a spell lasts, such as Instantaneous, 1 minute, or until dispelled. Some durations require Concentration.
entries.whatItMeans: Duration states how long a spell lasts, such as Instantaneous, 1 minute, or until dispelled. Some durations require Concentration.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Concentration spell lasting up to 1 minute ends early if Concentration breaks.
entries.whyItMatters: Tracking duration prevents effects from lasting too long or ending too early.

entries.title: Casting at a Higher Level
entries.summary: Some spells gain additional effects when cast using a slot above their normal level, as described in the spell.
entries.whatItMeans: Some spells gain additional effects when cast using a slot above their normal level, as described in the spell.
entries.exampleInPlay: A 1st-level spell might deal an extra die when cast with a 2nd-level slot.
entries.whyItMatters: Upcasting trades a stronger slot for a stronger version of a lower-level spell.

entries.title: Sorcery Points and Magical Pools
entries.summary: Some classes and features use a separate pool of points to modify spells or activate magical abilities.
entries.whatItMeans: Some classes and features use a separate pool of points to modify spells or activate magical abilities.
entries.exampleInPlay: A Sorcerer records current Sorcery Points and the Metamagic options that spend them.
entries.whyItMatters: Clear resource tracking prevents accidental overuse.

entries.title: Inspiration (2014)
entries.summary: 2014 Inspiration is a reward the DM can grant for roleplaying. A character can spend it to gain Advantage on an attack roll, saving throw, or ability check.
entries.whatItMeans: 2014 Inspiration is a reward the DM can grant for roleplaying. A character can spend it to gain Advantage on an attack roll, saving throw, or ability check.
entries.exampleInPlay: Spend Inspiration before making an important saving throw to roll with Advantage.
entries.whyItMatters: It rewards playing the character's personality and story.

entries.title: Heroic Inspiration (2024)
entries.summary: Heroic Inspiration lets a character reroll a die immediately after rolling it and use the new result. A character can hold only one Heroic Inspiration at a time.
entries.whatItMeans: Heroic Inspiration lets a character reroll a die immediately after rolling it and use the new result. A character can hold only one Heroic Inspiration at a time.
entries.exampleInPlay: After rolling poorly on a crucial save, spend Heroic Inspiration to reroll the die.
entries.whyItMatters: It provides a flexible second chance and should be recorded when gained or spent.

entries.title: Advantage and Disadvantage
entries.summary: With Advantage, roll two d20s and use the higher. With Disadvantage, roll two and use the lower. Multiple sources normally do not stack.
entries.whatItMeans: With Advantage, roll two d20s and use the higher. With Disadvantage, roll two and use the lower. Multiple sources normally do not stack.
entries.exampleInPlay: A hidden attacker with Advantage rolls two d20s and uses the higher result.
entries.whyItMatters: These rules change reliability without adding another numerical modifier.
